summary: This experimental memo defines Candidate Access Router Discovery. A mobile device uses it to learn which nearby access routers could take over its connection and what they can do, before a handover begins.

eli5.summary: When your phone moves, it should know which towers nearby could take over. This protocol lets it find out and ask in advance.

how does a mobile node find access routers for handover
how does a mobile node discover candidate routers before handover

subtitle: Protocol for mobile devices to discover and evaluate handover candidates before switching access routers

tldr.problem: Mobile nodes need to switch between access routers as they move, but they cannot make optimal handover decisions without knowing which routers are nearby and what services each offers.
tldr.mechanism: CARD allows a mobile node to ask its current router for the IP addresses and capabilities of candidate routers whose wireless access points it can hear, and to optionally request certificates for security validation.
tldr.outcome: Mobile devices can evaluate handover options in advance and choose a target router with matching capabilities, reducing latency and packet loss during the handover.

today: RFC 4066 is an Experimental protocol designed to improve seamless IP mobility. It remains unobsoleted and forms part of the work on fast mobile handover, though wider deployment depends on the uptake of seamless mobility protocols like Fast Mobile IPv6.

sections.title: Why Mobile Nodes Need Candidate Router Discovery
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 and similar protocols allow a device to maintain connectivity as it moves between networks. When a mobile node detects a new access point using its wireless interface (through link-layer scanning), it must decide whether to initiate a handover to that network. Seamless handover requires knowing which access routers are reachable, what services they support, and whether they meet the node's requirements.

Without pre-handover discovery, a mobile node must wait until after it associates with a new access point to learn the corresponding router's IP address and capabilities. This incurs delay and may cause temporary traffic loss. The CARD protocol allows the mobile node to learn this information while still connected to its current router, speeding handover decisions and enabling the use of fast handover protocols.
sections.eli5: You are at home using WiFi. Your phone scans the area and finds other towers. Before you even move, you ask your home router about those towers: where are they, how fast are they, what do they support? Then when you walk out the door, your phone already knows which tower is best and connects faster.

sections.title: Two-Step CARD Protocol Flow
sections.content:
CARD divides discovery into two separate message exchanges. In the MN-AR exchange, the mobile node sends a CARD Request to its current access router containing one or more Layer-2 identifiers (L2 IDs—for example, WiFi MAC addresses) of candidate access points. The current router maps each L2 ID to a candidate router's IP address using its local CAR table and optionally discovers the capabilities of those candidate routers. The current router then sends back a CARD Reply with the resolved IP addresses and (if requested) the candidates' capabilities.

In the optional AR-AR exchange, the current router queries candidate routers directly to obtain fresh capability information. The candidate router sends back its capabilities as attribute-value pairs. This allows the current router to maintain up-to-date information about candidates and answer MN requests quickly from its local cache rather than querying candidates on each request.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Your phone says to your current router, I see towers with these MAC addresses; tell me their IP addresses and speeds. Your current router looks them up and sends back the answer. Step 2 (optional): Your current router also calls those towers independently to ask for their latest status, keeping a list so it can answer faster next time.

sections.title: Reverse Address Translation and L2-L3 Mapping
sections.content:
Access routers maintain a CAR table—a mapping from Layer-2 identifiers (like AP MAC addresses) to Layer-3 IP addresses and capability information. When a mobile node sends an L2 ID for an access point, the current router performs reverse address translation: it looks up the L2 ID in the CAR table and returns the IP address of the associated candidate router.

If multiple L2 IDs map to the same candidate router (because one router operates multiple access points), the current router returns a MATCH status code pointing to a previously resolved address to avoid sending duplicate information. If an L2 ID cannot be resolved, the router returns a RESOLVER ERROR. If the mobile node sends no L2 IDs, the router sends back the L2 IDs and addresses of all candidate routers, marked as CANDIDATE in the status field, allowing the node to learn all available options.
sections.eli5: Think of it as a phone book. Your router knows: MAC address 00:11:22:33:44:55 belongs to the fast tower at 2001:db8::1, MAC address 00:11:22:33:44:66 belongs to the same tower. Your phone says, I see 44:55. Your router says, that is tower 2001:db8::1, and by the way, 44:66 is the same tower.

sections.title: Capability Discovery and Filtering
sections.content:
CARD capability information is encoded as attribute-value pairs conveyed in a Capability Container. Capabilities can represent anything of interest to the mobile node: available bandwidth, supported access technologies (802.11a, 802.11g), QoS guarantees, network load, or router features.

A mobile node can request only certain capabilities by including a Preferences sub-option listing the attribute types it cares about. It can also filter candidate routers using a Requirements sub-option, specifying attribute-value pairs that define cutoff thresholds—for example, minimum bandwidth or maximum latency. The current router uses these hints to perform optional pre-filtering, returning only candidates that match the node's preferences and requirements. Routers that do not implement filtering simply ignore these sub-options and return all information.
sections.eli5: You tell your router: I only care about 802.11a towers with at least 20 Mbps. Your router sends back only towers that match your criteria, not wasting your phone's battery showing you towers that would not be useful.

sections.title: Certificate-Based Validation and Security
sections.content:
CARD allows a mobile node to request and verify router certificates before committing to a handover. The MN can include a list of trusted certificate authorities in the CARD Request. The current router replies with a certification path anchored at one of the trusted anchors, with each certificate in a separate CARD Reply message. The MN uses this chain to verify the AR's public key and validate signatures on CARD and other mobility messages.

Routers use IPsec security associations to authenticate AR-AR CARD messages, ensuring that capability updates are genuine. Between the MN and current AR, CARD messages are transported using ICMP, which offers no built-in security, so the MN must validate certificates and signatures on critical CARD information. The RFC notes potential denial-of-service risks if the control connection is compromised and recommends that deployment policies restrict which routers can send CARD information to prevent spoofing attacks.
sections.eli5: Your phone asks for a proof that the towers are who they claim to be. The current tower passes you signed documents that prove the candidate towers' identity. Your phone checks the signatures using a trusted authority's key, making sure nobody is impersonating a fast tower and tricking you into a slow one.
